findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: External quality assessment of internal audit function is eight years overdue and scheduled only for consideration in 2026/27
findings.detail: Standards require external assessment every five years. North Tyneside's last external assessment was February 2018. The council acknowledges non-conformance but assesses the risk as low given annual self-assessment.
findings.matters: External validation of internal audit quality is required assurance; without it there is no independent assessment whether the audit function itself is operating effectively
findings.figures: Last external assessment: February 2018; standard requirement: every five years
findings.quote: This is required every five years, but North Tyneside's Internal Audit service was last subject to external assessment in February 2018.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit activity was resourced below the agreed plan for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council had fewer internal audit resources available during the year than established when the annual plan was agreed in May 2025. This directly reduced audit coverage compared to what was intended.
findings.matters: Reduced audit capacity means less independent oversight of financial controls; this narrows the probability of detecting control failures or financial irregularities
findings.figures: Resource levels reduced mid-year; shortfall magnitude not quantified
findings.quote: The overall level of resources available for internal audit activity during 2025/26 was less than that established when agreeing the annual plan in May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Home care payment system control weaknesses as delegation and review processes embed on new platform
findings.detail: The adult social care payment system received limited assurance due to incomplete implementation of delegation schemes and review procedures. The audit explicitly notes the system is 'still relatively new and arrangements are evolving,' indicating controls remain in development phase.
findings.matters: Adult social care typically represents a significant proportion of council spend; incomplete controls on a new financial system present material implementation risk until fully embedded
findings.figures: One of seven limited assurance opinions issued in 2025/26
findings.quote: Home Care Payment Arrangements – the matters relate to implementing a local scheme of delegation within the software used to manage payments and review of activity managed through this system. The system is still relatively new and arrangements are evolving.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26
findings.headline: Supplier database maintenance has limited assurance due to incomplete system implementation and underdeveloped fraud controls
findings.detail: The creditors audit found that the new system is not fully utilising its functionality and anti-fraud arrangements are not adequately developed. This represents a control gap in a core financial function at a time when the council faces acknowledged financial pressures.
findings.matters: Creditor controls are fundamental to preventing fraud and ensuring accurate financial reporting; weaknesses here create risk of undetected errors or fraudulent payments
findings.figures: One of seven limited assurance opinions issued in 2025/26
findings.quote: Creditors (suppliers database maintenance) – the matters relate to the implementation of the new system, not utilising all functionality and need to develop anti-fraud arrangements which are specific to this area

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: Council must develop action plan to address strategic recommendations from Independent Financial Resilience Review during 2026/27
findings.detail: The AGS action plan explicitly requires development of an action plan to meet recommendations from the Financial Resilience Review, to be incorporated into performance and finance reports to Cabinet. Target completion is during 2026/27.
findings.matters: Active remediation of external financial pressure recommendations is required; absence of a completed plan indicates the resilience issues remain unresolved.
findings.figures: 2026/27 financial year
findings.quote: Develop an Action Plan to meet the Strategic Recommendations set out in the Independent Financial Resilience Review Report and for that Plan to be incorporated into the Performance and Finance reports presented to Cabinet

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: Three consecutive years (2022/23–2024/25) of disclaimed external audit opinions on financial statements
findings.detail: The council's accounts have received disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years. The council states this reflects a national backlog issue and advises that external auditors confirmed this is not reflective of governance or financial management concerns specific to the authority.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions prevent independent verification of financial statements; even if due to national issues, this limits assurance over reported financial position.
findings.quote: Recent opinions, 2022/23 to 2024/25 have had disclaimed audit opinions which are reflective of issues related to a national backlog across the sector

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: Chief Internal Auditor gave qualified 'reasonable assurance' opinion, indicating improvements needed in some areas
findings.detail: Internal audit opinion for 2025/26 is 'reasonable assurance' rather than unqualified assurance, described as 'a positive opinion but reflecting improvements are required in some areas'. This is a qualified opinion signalling control weaknesses exist.
findings.matters: Qualified internal audit opinions indicate control gaps exist within governance and financial management arrangements that require remediation.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The indicative opinion for 2025/26 is 'Reasonable assurance' which is a positive opinion but reflecting improvements are required in some areas

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: Independent Financial Resilience Review found council managing 'very challenging position' with 'external pressures that drive financial risk'
findings.detail: North Tyneside commissioned a CIPFA Independent Financial Resilience Review during 2025/26. That review noted the council's strong governance has enabled it to manage a difficult financial situation, but specifically stated these strengths 'do not, however, insulate the Council from the external pressures that drive its financial risk.'
findings.matters: A council explicitly flagged as facing external financial pressures and a challenging position is material information for any lender assessing credit risk; the council has commissioned external assessment of financial sustainability.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: These strengths are material and explain why the Council has been able to manage a very challenging position without governance failure. They do not, however, insulate the Council from the external pressures that drive its financial risk

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 2025-26 Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: General Fund capital receipts reduced from £2.62m to £1.59m
findings.detail: Capital funding available from asset disposals declined by 39%. This reduces the council's ability to self-fund capital projects and increases reliance on borrowing, grants, or revenue contributions.
findings.matters: Falling capital receipts can signal difficulty in disposing of assets or reduced asset sales, and it shifts the financing burden onto borrowing or revenue, both of which have tighter constraints.
findings.figures: £2.620m (approved) → £1.586m (revised)
findings.quote: Capital Receipts 2.620 1.586

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 2025-26 Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision jumped 27.9% to £16.84m, driven by IFRS 16 lease accounting
findings.detail: The General Fund's annual MRP charge increased from £13.2m to £16.84m. The revised estimate includes £1.937m of new IFRS 16 MRP provision and an increase in leases/PFI MRP from £3.414m to £5.225m, reflecting the council's lease and PFI commitments under new accounting standards.
findings.matters: Higher MRP locks in future revenue commitments and reduces flexibility; the scale of the IFRS 16 adjustment reveals the size of lease/PFI obligations the council carries that were previously off-balance-sheet.
findings.figures: £13.2m → £16.84m (General Fund); IFRS 16 MRP Provision £1.937m; Leases/PFI MRP £3.414m → £5.225m
findings.quote: Total Projected MRP Charge 13.200 16.840; IFRS 16 MRP Provision 1.937

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 2025-26 Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: General Fund financing costs ratio increased to 12.72% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: The proportion of the council's General Fund revenue consumed by financing costs rose from 11.35% to 12.72%. This means the council has proportionally less revenue available for service delivery as debt servicing takes a larger share.
findings.matters: A rising financing costs ratio indicates reduced fiscal flexibility; a lender would want to know if this trajectory continues and what it signals about the council's capital strategy.
findings.figures: 11.35% (approved 2025/26) → 12.72% (revised 2025/26); General Fund net revenue stream
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream General Fund 11.35% 12.72%

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 outturn - Outturn Financial Summary
findings.headline: High interest rate environment (Bank Rate 3.75%, PWLB 50-year at 6.58%) is increasing capital financing costs and constraining investment affordability
findings.detail: With Bank Rate held at 3.75% and long-term PWLB rates elevated (50-year at 6.58%), the council's capital borrowing costs have risen permanently. The authority notes that this high-rate environment impacts the revenue budget for schemes requiring prudential borrowing. The council's under-borrowed position has halved from £39.231m to £26.773m as it externalised borrowing; it took £20m short-term PWLB borrowing in April 2025.
findings.matters: Sustained high interest rates mean the council faces a permanent increase in capital financing costs. With structural deficits already constraining revenue flexibility, higher borrowing costs reduce investment capacity and increase the proportion of revenue budget consumed by debt service.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; PWLB 50-year 6.58%; under-borrowed position £26.773m (halved from £39.231m); £20m short-term PWLB borrowing in April 2025; total outstanding borrowing £520.443m
findings.quote: A high-rate interest environment has an impact on the Authority's revenue budget and schemes within the Investment Plan requiring the use of prudential borrowing. At its meeting ending on 29 April 2026, the MPC voted by a majority of 8-1 to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 outturn - Outturn Financial Summary
findings.headline: Adults services commissioned care budget overshot by £3.165m; staff recruitment and retention remain unresolved structural issues
findings.detail: Adults services reported a £2.167m overspend on £75.135m budget. Operational costs came in £1.006m under due to delayed restructures, but commissioned services (mainly external older persons and physical disability care) overshot by £3.165m. The council reports ongoing problems with recruitment and retention of Adult Services staff and is relying on maximising external funding and client contributions to manage the budget.
findings.matters: A social services directorate unable to control commissioned care spend while facing staff retention problems is heading toward a position where internal capacity cannot be built and external spending cannot be contained.
findings.figures: £2.167m overall overspend; commissioned services overspend £3.165m on £58.073m budget; operational staffing underspend of £1.006m despite recruitment/retention problems
findings.quote: The operational costs of the service are reporting an underspend for 2025/26 of £1.006m, a reduction of £0.251m since the January forecast. The movement reflects assumptions made during 2025/26 around recovery of staff costs from external funding. The overall underspend continues to reflect the delay of service restructures taking place in 2025/26 while consultation is finalised. These changes will help drive out efficiency targets as well as address the backlog in reviews and assessments. This will continue to be closely monitored throughout 2026/27 as problems with recruitment and retention of staff across Adult Services has previously been an issue.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 outturn - Outturn Financial Summary
findings.headline: Housing disrepair claims from law firms targeting social landlords are escalating costs; new electrical safety regulations add £0.5m compliance pressure
findings.detail: The council reports systematic targeting by legal disrepair claim firms, driving higher costs for legal fees, accelerated remedial works, and compensation. Separately, new Social Housing Quality and Safety regulations mandate Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICR) on a five-year cycle (halved from ten years). Contractor rates are elevated to meet volume and time pressures, and inspections are discovering more defects requiring remedial action. The council estimates £0.5m additional pressure to comply within the required timeframe.
findings.matters: A social housing provider cannot easily pass disrepair claims or accelerated compliance costs to tenants through rent. These are structural cost pressures driven by regulation and litigation that will persist and are difficult to forecast.
findings.figures: £0.5m estimated pressure for EICR compliance in a five-year cycle; unquantified but escalating disrepair legal and compensation costs
findings.quote: Disrepair costs have increased significantly due to the growing activity of legal disrepair claim firms targeting social landlords.  As a result, we are facing higher costs from legal fees, accelerated remedial works, and compensation payments—often for issues that could have been resolved more efficiently through standard repairs channels. This trend is placing places additional financial pressure on housing budgets and complicates service delivery. To ensure compliance within the required timeframe there is an estimated £0.5m pressure in this area.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 outturn - Outturn Financial Summary
findings.headline: Schools High Needs funding deficit £13.545m; 25 schools are in deficit, three holding catastrophic individual deficits of £2-7m each
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs block deficit grew from £11.502m to £13.545m despite £1.950m Safety Valve funding (which is now ending). Twenty-five of 57 maintained schools are in deficit totalling £17.479m. Three schools hold deficits alone totalling £12.713m: Monkseaton High £6.682m, Norham £3.767m, Beacon Hill £2.264m. The DSG is ring-fenced, so any deficit must be carried forward; it cannot be repaid from general fund reserves.
findings.matters: High Needs deficits signal that the council cannot fund statutory SEND provision. Safety Valve funding ends April 2026. The new High Needs Stability Grant will offset deficits against other DSG surpluses, but if the deficit persists and surpluses are exhausted, the council faces a structural overspend it cannot control.
findings.figures: DSG ring-fenced account deficit £11.231m; High Needs block deficit £13.545m (up from £11.502m); 25 schools in deficit totalling £17.479m; three schools with deficits over £2m each; Safety Valve funding of £1.950m now ended
findings.quote: After allowing for school funding allocations, the 2025/26 DSG ring-fenced account is showing a net deficit balance of £11.231m. The High Needs block 2024/25 outturn was a deficit of £11.502m and this pressure has continued in 2025/26 with a provisional in-year deficit of £3.994m, however this has been partially off-set by £1.950m Safety Valve funding from the DfE.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 outturn - Outturn Financial Summary
findings.headline: Children's placements overshot by £10.064m as external care costs rose 17% in one year, with no evidence of pressure easing
findings.detail: Children in care grew to 419 against a 400-child budget, forcing greater reliance on expensive external placements. Average weekly costs for external children's homes jumped from £5,945 in 2023/24 to £6,981 by March 2026. The entire £10.064m overspend is driven by placement costs escalating beyond assumptions. The council has no control over demand and cannot refuse to house children; costs are set by a market of private providers.
findings.matters: This is a statutory demand-led service where the council cannot constrain costs. If placement inflation continues at 17% per year and child numbers keep rising, this will become a structural deficit that cannot be managed within the social services budget.
findings.figures: £10.064m overspend; 419 children in care vs 400 budgeted; external children's homes budget £12.889m vs outturn £22.805m (£9.916m over); average weekly placement cost £6,981 vs £5,945 in 2023/24
findings.quote: The number of children in our care in March 2026 continued to grow to 419, (this is an increase of 19 from previously reported) with the number of children in external children's homes remaining higher than budgeted for. The high number of children in our care is leading to sufficiency pressures and an increased reliance on external care arrangements. Market forces and increasing costs of external placements continue to impact on the pressure within external children's homes, the average weekly cost during 2023/24 was £5,945 and is currently £6,981

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account collection at 94.12% with rising arrears and bankruptcies
findings.detail: HRA rental income collection stands at 94.12%, with the report noting that 'Arrears management continues to be a critical area of performance' and citing 'an increase in the number of bankruptcies which require arrears to be written off.' Drivers include increased Universal Credit migration, cost of living pressures, and reduced support for under-occupation.
findings.matters: HRA revenue collection is critical to the Housing Revenue Account's ability to service its debt and maintain services. Deteriorating collection rates, driven by cost of living and welfare changes, signal income risk.
findings.figures: 94.12% collection rate, increasing arrears, increasing bankruptcies
findings.quote: Arrears management continues to be a critical area of performance, and officers are monitoring increasing arrears levels alongside an increase in the number of bankruptcies which require arrears to be written off.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Adult Services overspend of £2.159m signals ongoing pressure on commissioned services
findings.detail: Adult Services ended the year with a £2.159m overspend despite £2.950m in planned savings for the year. The report explicitly notes that 'complexity of care and continued demand pressures have meant pressure on commissioned services continues.' This is a structural overspend, not a one-off.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a core council service and a major budget item. Growing demand and pressure on commissioned services, despite savings efforts, suggests the council's cost base is not aligned with service need.
findings.figures: £2.159m overspend, £2.950m savings achieved but insufficient to prevent overspend
findings.quote: complexity of care and continued demand pressures have meant pressure on commissioned services continues.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit of £13.545m growing as EHCP demand rises 16%
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs block has a cumulative deficit of £13.545m. Requests for EHCP assessments are rising 16%, and EHCPs issued also rose 16%, higher than both regional (10.67%) and national (9.8%) averages. Safety Valve programme funding ends 1 April 2026, moving to a different grant mechanism. The underlying demand trend is adverse.
findings.matters: Growing high needs demand and a large DSG deficit creates a contingent liability for the council. The move away from Safety Valve means less certainty in funding, and demand growth exceeds regional and national trends, suggesting structural rather than cyclical issues.
findings.figures: £13.545m High Needs deficit, 16% increase in EHCPs issued, 16% increase in assessment requests, 2,714 total EHCPs
findings.quote: EHCPs issued also rose by 16% at the end of March 2026 to total 2,714, higher than the regional (10.67%) and national (9.8%) trends in 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Schools sector collective deficit worsening, not improving
findings.detail: Maintained schools' collective deficit deteriorated from -£4.337m to -£7.716m (a £3.4m worsening). Two-fifths of schools (25 of 57) ended the year with a cumulative deficit, and a further 34 schools reported an in-year deficit. Monkseaton High School is closing with a £6.682m cumulative deficit. The sector is not stabilising.
findings.matters: A large and growing schools deficit indicates structural issues in the education system that the council may need to fund. This is a contingent liability and a sign of underlying demand/funding misalignment.
findings.figures: Collective deficit -£7.716m (from -£4.337m), 25 of 57 schools in cumulative deficit, 34 in in-year deficit, Monkseaton £6.682m deficit
findings.quote: Collective school balances in Authority maintained schools decreased further from a deficit of £4.337m at the start of the year to a closing deficit of £7.716m.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Strategic Reserve being drawn down for unplanned use to balance the budget
findings.detail: The council is using £1.115m from its Strategic Reserve to balance 2025/26. While the report states this is planned to be replenished, the draw is unplanned and reflects the underlying deficit. The reserve stands at only £4.885m after this transfer, providing limited buffer for future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserves are being used as a lever to balance budgets rather than held as contingency. This reduces financial flexibility and indicates the council is relying on reserves rather than structural cost control.
findings.figures: £1.115m withdrawal from Strategic Reserve, reserve balance £4.885m after transfer
findings.quote: This report sets out the proposed release of £1.115m from the Strategic Reserve to support the year end position.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Three key MTFP savings workstreams are delayed and costs are rising
findings.detail: Over £14m of savings were planned across 14 workstreams for 2025/26, but three critical areas are now reporting delays and cost increases: children's finance, people and workforce, and commissioning. These are not minor projects; they form a core part of the council's deficit reduction strategy and the delays indicate the savings plans are not working as designed.
findings.matters: Failing savings plans are a red flag for a lender. If the council cannot deliver its planned savings, the budget position will deteriorate further. This affects the medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £14m of savings planned, three workstreams with delays and cost increases
findings.quote: Challenges remain in MTFP 07 - Handling Children's Finance, MTFP 12 – People and Workforce and MTFP 14 – Commissioning, with savings being delayed and costs continuing to increase.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Children's services overspend growing as child numbers reach record highs
findings.detail: Children's Services ended 2025/26 with a £10.064m overspend, with 419 children in care by March (the highest level reached). The pressure is concentrated: 50 children in external children's homes accounted for £9.592m of the directorate's overspend. Child numbers are not stabilising; they reached 400 in January and climbed further to 419 by March, indicating continuing demand growth.
findings.matters: This is a structural, growing demand pressure that the council is struggling to manage. External placements are expensive and the trend is upward. This directly affects the council's ability to balance budgets going forward.
findings.figures: £10.064m overspend, 419 children in care at 31 March 2026 (400 in January), 50 in external homes costing £9.592m
findings.quote: The Authority continues to have high number of children in its care, which reached its highest level of 400 in January 2026 and continued to climb to 419 by 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Performance and Financial Management Outturn Report to 31 March 2026
findings.headline: One-off dividend of £6.6m masks underlying structural deficit of £7.7m
findings.detail: The reported £1.115m overspend was achieved only through a one-off dividend from Newcastle International Airport shareholding. The S151 officer's own analysis states that without this non-recurring income, the overspend would have been £7.7m. This reveals a significant underlying budget gap that is being masked by asset income rather than resolved through savings or service reform.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's structural financial position, not its one-off-adjusted position. A £7.7m structural deficit is a material issue for creditworthiness and repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £6.6m dividend, £7.7m would-be overspend without it, actual reported overspend £1.115m
findings.quote: Without this one-off income, the overspend would have been significantly higher at £7.7m, emphasizing the continued need to deliver the savings identified within the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: North Tyneside Council- Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Auditors require additional evidence and transaction listings not previously demanded
findings.detail: Management must provide evidence and transaction listings beyond what is normally required, as part of the rebuilding assurance strategy. This indicates the council's standard financial records and documentation are insufficient for normal audit purposes.
findings.matters: The need for exceptional additional evidence signals fundamental weaknesses in the financial control environment and suggests the council's records do not meet standard governance expectations.
findings.figures: Programme spans planning (March-April 2026), interim work (May-August 2026), fieldwork (September-December 2026)
findings.quote: We have initiated discussions with management on the evidence and transaction listings we will require as this is likely to involve additional and different information which has not been required previously in order to for us to have sufficient appropriate evidence upon which to form an opinion

findings.paper_title: North Tyneside Council- Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council will receive qualified opinions for 2025/26 and 2026/27; clean opinion not until 2027/28
findings.detail: The rebuilding assurance programme projects qualified (not clean) opinions for the next two years, with an unmodified opinion only expected by 2027/28. This multi-year recovery path indicates deep, systemic issues with financial records and the audit evidence base.
findings.matters: A multi-year path to a clean opinion signals persistent weaknesses in financial control and record-keeping that cannot be fixed quickly, presenting ongoing risk to stakeholders.
findings.figures: 2025/26 qualified (deadline 30 January 2027); 2026/27 qualified (deadline 30 November 2027); 2027/28 unmodified (deadline 30 November 2028)
findings.quote: The audit team no longer needs to disclaim as it has regained assurance over the closing balance sheet. However, it qualifies all other primary statements due to a lack of assurance over the opening position which has the potential to impact the current year CIES, MIRS and Cash Flow.

findings.paper_title: North Tyneside Council- Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Lack of assurance over opening balances creates uncertainty about reserve balances
findings.detail: The disclaimer on 2024/25 means auditors have no assurance over opening balances for 2025/26, creating particular challenges for reserve balances since these reflect prior-year transactions and required accounting classifications. The council cannot certify the accuracy of its reserves.
findings.matters: Reserves are critical to financial resilience; uncertainty about their accuracy undermines understanding of the council's ability to manage unexpected costs or financial stress.
findings.figures: Impact extends to reserve classification for 2025/26 financial statements
findings.quote: We do not have assurance over all opening balances for the 2025/26 financial statements. This absence of assurance relating to previous years presents particular challenges in relation to reserve balances as these reflect transactions posted in earlier years

findings.paper_title: North Tyneside Council- Audit Progress Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Three consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25)
findings.detail: The council's accounts for three consecutive years have received disclaimed audit opinions, meaning the auditors cannot provide assurance that the financial statements are accurate or complete. The most recent disclaimer was issued in February 2026. Without audited accounts, there is no reliable basis for assessing the council's financial position.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess credit risk or understand the council's true financial health without audited statements; this signals fundamental control and reporting problems.
findings.figures: 2022/23 disclaimed 9 December 2024; 2023/24 disclaimed 20 February 2024; 2024/25 disclaimed 26 February 2026
findings.quote: In February 2026, we disclaimed our opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements. This followed on from disclaimed opinions issued previously in respect of the Council's 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts.

findings.paper_title: Council 2026-2030 Financial Planning and Budget Process - Cover Report
findings.headline: Capital investment programme of £352.265m over five years funded through prudential borrowing
findings.detail: The council proposes a five-year investment plan from 2026/27 to 2030/31 totalling £352.265m, with all projects subject to full gateway and governance procedures. This is significant given current reserve constraints.
findings.matters: A substantial borrowing programme combined with low reserves and emerging revenue pressures increases refinancing risk and reduces headroom for economic shocks.
findings.figures: £352.265m planned investment 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.quote: planned investment of £352.265m from 2026/27 to 2030/31

findings.paper_title: Council 2026-2030 Financial Planning and Budget Process - Cover Report
findings.headline: Several significant financial risks have emerged since February 2025 affecting the current year and 2026/27
findings.detail: The CFO reports that since the 2025/26 budget was set, further significant risks have emerged impacting both the 2025/26 position and increasing pressures for 2026/27. These include social care demand, pay awards, and inflation, with contingencies set at £1.402m.
findings.matters: Emerging pressures mid-year that force upward revisions to the following year's budget suggest structural cost issues (particularly in social care) that may not be fully addressed by current plans.
findings.figures: £1.402m contingency for 2026/27, emerging pressures in social care, pay awards, and inflation
findings.quote: Since the development of the 2025/26 Budget and Medium-Term Financial Plan in February 2025, several further significant risks have emerged that are impacting on the 2025/26 budget position, as well as increasing the pressure identified for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Council 2026-2030 Financial Planning and Budget Process - Cover Report
findings.headline: Strategic Reserve has fallen below the council's own £10m minimum target
findings.detail: The council identifies that sustained pressures in recent years have depleted its Strategic Reserve below its own policy target of £10m. The budget proposes replenishment of £2.25m in 2026/27 and £2.5m annually thereafter, but this is aspirational given emerging pressures.
findings.matters: A council operating below its own defined minimum reserve threshold signals constrained financial flexibility and a reliance on sustained service delivery improvements to rebuild buffers.
findings.figures: £10m target, £2.25m planned replenishment 2026/27, £2.5m planned annually thereafter
findings.quote: The sustained pressures experienced in recent years have seen the Authority's Strategic Reserve fall below the Authority's own target level of £10m.

findings.paper_title: Council 2026-2030 Financial Planning and Budget Process - Cover Report
findings.headline: Schools held a net deficit of £12.952m that could fall to the General Fund
findings.detail: Maintained schools balances are forecast to show a deficit of £12.952m as at 31 March 2026, including material individual school deficits. The council notes these 'could ultimately fall on General Fund balances if they cannot be resolved in conjunction with the individual schools.'
findings.matters: A material contingent liability of this scale significantly reduces effective council reserves and could require emergency action or further borrowing if schools cannot resolve deficits independently.
findings.figures: £12.952m net deficit forecast at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: This is forecast to be a net deficit figure of £12.952m as at 31 March 2026, which includes a range of surplus and deficit balances for individual schools, some of which are material deficit balances. These could ultimately fall on General Fund balances if they cannot be resolved in conjunction with the individual schools.

findings.paper_title: Council 2026-2030 Financial Planning and Budget Process - Cover Report
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are at a minimum level despite emerging 2025/26 pressures
findings.detail: The council brought forward £37.5m into 2025/26 but faces a forecast November 2025 outturn deficit of £6.2m, which if met from reserves would reduce available 2026/27 reserves to £29.7m. The CFO explicitly states reserves are 'relatively low and at a minimum level' when considering risks faced and efficiencies required.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb unexpected pressures or service shocks without compromising service delivery or requiring further borrowing.
findings.figures: £37.5m brought forward 2025/26, £35.9m expected 2026/27, £6.2m forecast 2025/26 outturn deficit, £29.7m projected after deficit
findings.quote: Reserves are relatively low and at a minimum level when considering the risks the Authority faces, and the level of efficiencies required to be achieved in the medium-term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio generating rental income but exposed to void periods and rental decline
findings.detail: The council owns a portfolio of tenanted non-operational units (industrial and retail units) that generate revenue income. The strategy identifies that the key risk exposure for this portfolio is void periods and reductions in rental income.
findings.matters: Rental income contributes to revenue funding, but economic downturns or property market weakness could reduce this income stream when the council is already facing revenue budget pressures.
findings.figures: No specific figures on rental income or portfolio size provided
findings.quote: The Authority does own a portfolio of tenanted non-operational units, such as industrial units and retail units which generate a source of revenue income, however these have been held for a number of years and are retained primarily to support the Authority's priorities around local employment and regeneration. As such, the key risk exposure relates to void periods and reductions in rental income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Substantial PFI liabilities of £131.3m not included in main Capital Financing Requirement projections
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2025, the council held £131.3m in long-term PFI scheme liabilities across four categories: Sheltered Accommodation (£82.9m), Schools (£24.6m), Joint Service Centres (£14.4m), and Street Lighting (£9.4m). These are separate from the CFR and borrowing figures and represent committed long-term revenue obligations.
findings.matters: These represent additional debt-like obligations on the revenue budget not reflected in the main borrowing projections; lenders need to understand the full picture of long-term financial commitments.
findings.figures: Total PFI liabilities: £131.271m; Sheltered Accommodation: £82.891m; Schools: £24.581m; Joint Service Centres: £14.448m; Street Lighting: £9.351m
findings.quote: As at 31st March 2025 the Council held £131.271m long-term liabilities in respect of PFI schemes; Sheltered Accommodation £82.891m; Schools £24.581m; Joint Service Centres £14.448m; Street Lighting £9.351m

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital strategy under significant pressure from sustained market volatility
findings.detail: The strategy document itself identifies that the capital strategy is under significant financial pressure as a result of sustained market volatility in recent years, requiring the strategy to include flexibility to respond to market changes and risks.
findings.matters: Acknowledged market volatility pressure indicates the council is already stretched; this adds risk to delivery of the capital plan and to the sustainability of borrowing costs.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Capital Strategy is under significant financial pressure as a result of sustained market volatility in recent years. The Strategy must therefore include an element of flexibility to respond to changes and risks within the market and manage resources effectively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Revenue budget pressures limiting the council's ability to use revenue funding for capital investment
findings.detail: The Capital Strategy explicitly notes that current revenue budget pressures constrain the General Fund's ability to directly finance capital expenditure. This limits financing flexibility and means the council must rely more heavily on external funding, capital receipts, and borrowing.
findings.matters: Revenue constraints reduce the council's buffer for capital financing and suggest wider financial stress; it indicates less capacity to fund capital without borrowing.
findings.figures: No specific figures given; statement applies to General Fund capital financing
findings.quote: Capital investment can be financed directly from the Authority's revenue budget. However, the current pressures on the Authority's revenue budget limit the extent of this type of funding in the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Strategic under-borrowing due to interest rate concerns, managing borrowing opportunistically rather than on schedule
findings.detail: The liability benchmark analysis shows the council is under-borrowed against its Capital Financing Requirement. Rather than borrowing all needed funds upfront, the council is deliberately under-borrowing, using internal cash resources to manage interest rate risk and avoid excessive borrowing costs. This means borrowing timing depends on rate conditions, not capital need.
findings.matters: This strategy indicates the council is rate-sensitive and has constrained cash reserves; inability to borrow when needed could delay capital projects, and it suggests existing treasury stress.
findings.figures: Additional borrowing required 2025/26-2035/36: £169.9m-£206.9m; Existing external debt 2025/26: £378.4m
findings.quote: The liability benchmark indicates that the Authority will be under-borrowed against its requirements. This will mean that additional borrowing will be required but the Authority will manage that by monitoring interest rates and identifying the optimum borrowing opportunities in accordance with its Treasury Management Strategy. There may be occasions when the Authority will opt to actively be under-borrowed to avoid excessive interest rate costs through the use of internal resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B(iv) - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Additional borrowing of £170m-£210m annually required to fund capital plan
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement for 2025/26 is £548.3m, and the council projects it will need additional external borrowing of £169.9m in 2025/26 rising to £206.9m by 2035/36 to support the approved capital investment plan. The Investment Plan itself is £344m over five years (£154m General Fund, £190m Housing Revenue Account).
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of future borrowing demand; this shows sustained large annual borrowing needs over a decade.
findings.figures: Additional External Debt Requirement: £169.863m (2025/26), £202.495m (2029/30), £206.983m (2035/36); Net Debt Charges: £19.352m-£21.968m annually; Total approved capital plan: £344m
findings.quote: The Investment Plan, approved by Council in February 2025 covers the period to 2029/30 and amounts to almost £344m, with £154m of General Fund schemes and £190m within the Housing Revenue Account.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: General Fund balance policy and reserve resilience being built incrementally but starting from £7m minimum
findings.detail: The MTFP includes a policy to maintain the General Fund Balance at a minimum level of £7m, with intention to increase over medium-term to ~5% of the Net Revenue Budget. The plan includes projected contributions to Strategic Reserve of £9.75m over four years and proposals to increase General Fund balance by £6m per annum from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial resilience partly through reserve coverage; a £7m minimum on a £267m budget is only 2.6% coverage, below recommended levels; building to 5% requires sustained annual contributions which may be at risk if pressures recur.
findings.figures: Minimum General Fund balance £7m; target ~5% of NRB; Strategic Reserve contributions £9.75m over 4 years; proposed £6m per annum increase from 2027/28
findings.quote: The Authority will maintain its General Fund Balance at a minimum level of £7m, with the intention of increasing this over the medium-term to a level of c.5% of the Net Revenue Budget, subject to a risk assessment as part of the annual budget-setting process

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: Significant grant restructuring with legacy grants rolled into Revenue Support Grant creates presentation change masking real-terms funding position
findings.detail: The Provisional Settlement announced 17 December 2025 involves major changes to grant distribution, with £49.48m of legacy grants rolled into Revenue Support Grant and £4.2m rolled into Specific Grants. This creates a large apparent increase in the Net Revenue Budget (from £206.5m to £267.4m) but restating 2025/26 on the same basis shows the real increase is only c.£7.4m. This represents a funding reform that reduces the visibility of how money is allocated.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether the council's financial improvement is real or a presentation change; the underlying funding position shows much tighter growth than nominal figures suggest.
findings.figures: £49.48m legacy grants rolled into RSG; £4.2m into Specific Grants; apparent NRB increase £60.9m but real increase ~£7.4m; CSP increase 5% (£13.4m)
findings.quote: Whilst this appears a significant increase, restating the 2025/26 budget on a similar basis to include legacy grants as a source of government funding would have increased the Net Revenue Budget from £206.5m to £260.0m, resulting in a proposed increase in the Authority's Net Revenue Budget of c.£7.4m between the two years.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: Pay awards increased to 3% per annum from 2% assumption, adding £3.5m pressure in 2026/27
findings.detail: The MTFP has been updated to include an uplift for pay awards at 3% per annum, rather than the 2% originally assumed from 2026/27 onwards. This is included in the People and Workforce Project and has an impact of £3.5m in 2026/27 alone.
findings.matters: Pay cost escalation beyond planning assumptions reduces budget flexibility; this is a structural cost increase that persists across the MTFP period and future years.
findings.figures: 3% pay award vs 2% assumed; £3.5m impact in 2026/27
findings.quote: Pay award – the MTFP has been updated to include an uplift for pay awards which now provides for a 3% per annum increase, rather than the 2% originally assumed from 2026/27 onwards. The impact of the assumed pay award on 2026/27 is £3.5m.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: General Fund capital financing costs £17.962m in 2026/27 with £63.677m new prudential borrowing planned
findings.detail: The council's capital financing costs are projected to be £17.962m in 2026/27, the majority related to historic capital investment. The draft Investment Plan assumes £63.677m of prudential borrowing for the General Fund over 2026-2031. Every £1m of borrowing costs approximately £0.1m per annum in revenue terms to meet financing costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt serviceability and trajectory of borrowing costs relative to net revenue budget; this constrains financial headroom available for service pressures.
findings.figures: Capital financing costs £17.962m 2026/27; £63.677m prudential borrowing 2026-2031; borrowing cost ratio ~£0.1m per £1m borrowed
findings.quote: The Authority's capital financing costs, excluding PFI schemes, are projected to be £17.962m in 2026/27. In broad terms, every £1m of borrowing costs the Authority circa £0.1m per annum in revenue terms

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: HRA debt currently £231.9m with ongoing borrowing to fund investment and maintenance
findings.detail: The HRA debt is expected to be £231.865m by end of March 2026, having been reduced by £58.960m since the start of self-financing in 2012/13. The 30-year business plan projects closing HRA debt of £124.926m, meaning £106.939m would be repaid over 30 years. However, the Investment Plan includes £13m of additional HRA borrowing over the next 5 years and substantial annual capital investment.
findings.matters: The scale of HRA borrowing and its repayment trajectory must be modelled against rental income sustainability and tenant payment capacity; Universal Credit roll-out is noted as creating ongoing pressure on tenants.
findings.figures: HRA debt £231.865m (31 March 2026); projected closing debt £124.926m over 30 years; £13m HRA borrowing 2026-2031; £168.564m revenue/major repairs funding for HRA capital 2026-2031
findings.quote: By the end of March 2026, the Authority's actual HRA debt is expected to be £231.865m, having been reduced by £58.960m since the start of self-financing. Based on the current approach to debt management it is estimated that up to a further £107m of debt could be repaid over the next 30 years.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: Adult Social Care facing £8m pressures driven by National Living Wage and market forces
findings.detail: The MTFP includes £8m of growth for Adult Social Care in 2026/27, primarily the impact of market forces which are directly impacted by rises in the National Living Wage. The council identifies that this is one of the key pressures impacting the Authority's 2026/27 Budget.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a statutory service with unbounded demand; escalating costs driven by external factors the council cannot control (National Living Wage) represents a structural budget risk.
findings.figures: £8m pressure in Adult Social Care 2026/27
findings.quote: Adult Social Care (£8m) – primarily the impact of market forces, which are directly impacted by rises in National Living wage

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: North Tyneside receives below-average funding on a per capita basis compared to peer councils
findings.detail: The council's Core Spending Power per capita for 2026/27 is £1,315, which is £79 lower than the North East average (£1,394) and £18 below the England average (£1,333). This represents a structural funding disadvantage equivalent to £16.9m for the borough as a whole versus North East peers and £3.9m versus England average.
findings.matters: A persistently lower funding baseline reduces the council's financial flexibility and headroom to manage unforeseen pressures or service demand variations compared to demographically similar councils.
findings.figures: North Tyneside £1,315 per capita; North East average £1,394; England average £1,333
findings.quote: Cabinet should note that on a per capita basis, CSP for 2026/27 equates to £1,315, which is £79 lower than the North East average (equating to £16.9m for the Borough as a whole) and £18 below the England average (equating to £3.9m for the Borough as a whole)

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: Maintained school sector carrying unabsorbed deficits now exceeding £15m
findings.detail: The council has identified a project to systematically review the education system because there are increasing levels of maintained school deficits. Without action, there is a risk the council would need to absorb this debt, which is currently in excess of £15m. An allocation of £0.7m has been added to the MTFP relating to the impact of the potential deficit linked to the closure of Monkseaton High School.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council may be forced to absorb substantial education sector liabilities that would materially impact its financial position and limit its flexibility.
findings.figures: School deficits in excess of £15m; £0.7m allocation for Monkseaton High School closure deficit
findings.quote: There are increasing levels of maintained school deficits. Without action, there is a risk we would need to absorb this debt, which is currently in excess of £15m

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 26 January 2026 - Budget Proposals Annex
findings.headline: Children's Social Care demand and cost pressures are significantly exceeding prior assumptions
findings.detail: The council has added £10m of growth to Children's Services in 2026/27 to address current demand and inflationary pressures of looked after children. This is £8m higher than the original 2026/27 assumption in the previous MTFP, reflecting additional complexity and market forces. The council attributes this to the impact of market forces on the costs of supporting looked after children.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand in statutory children's services is a material budget risk that constrains all other discretionary spending and can trigger service deficits; a lender needs to see this is managed and forecasting is robust.
findings.figures: £10m added in 2026/27; £8m higher than previously assumed
findings.quote: Growth of over £10m has been added to Children's Services to address current demand and inflationary pressures of our looked after children. This is £8m higher than the original 2026/27 assumption in the previous MTFP, reflecting the additional complexity and market forces

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Statement and Credit Criteria
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement not fully funded with loan debt; reserves being used as a temporary measure
findings.detail: The council is using cash from reserves and balances to fund capital needs rather than taking out sufficient loan debt. The paper acknowledges this is temporary and notes the council needs to review borrowing strategy as interest rates change.
findings.matters: Lenders would be concerned about reserve depletion and whether the council can fund future capital needs or refinance when reserves run out. This creates refinancing risk if rates rise.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures given in this extract
findings.quote: The Authority's capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement) has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.
